summary.text:
The largest discount position we have seen. Cumberland's own Q3 appendix records a net premature redemption discount of £37.098m — £3.178m of premia against £40.276m of discounts — on a £282.067m book. The PWLB redemption value of £230.512m against £265.969m of principal says the same thing from the other direction. This is a book largely written before rates rose, averaging 3.69% on the PWLB with over twenty years still to run.

What makes it interesting is not the size but the movement. The same figure was £38.416m at 31 March 2025, £43.726m at 30 September and £37.098m at 31 December: a £6.6m swing inside a single quarter. A number that moves that much between reports is a number worth seeing daily rather than quarterly. No rescheduling took place in the quarter.

Alongside that, the near end has filled up: £41.315m now falls due inside twelve months against £1.304m a year earlier. One caution before anything is used externally — their (under)/over borrowing line does not reconcile to the CFR and borrowing figures in this appendix, and the c.£110m gap looks like other long-term liabilities inside their gross debt measure. No internal-borrowing figure should be quoted for Cumberland until we hold the annual report.

officer.body:
Hi Barry,

Apologies for the cold email. PWLBtoday is fairly new so you may not have come across us yet.

We're built for local authority treasury teams and nothing else: live PWLB rates at both daily fixings, a monthly breakdown of every loan the sector draws, every council's PWLB book priced daily against the DMO's repayment curve, and a training academy for officers and members. There's more — the predictor, the SONIA path, peer metrics, a daily brief — in the brochure at [BROCHURE URL]. We don't sell treasury products, and the data side is free and stays free.

To keep that data and our training relevant we built tools that watch committee papers across every council in the country, so we can see how a council's own figures compare with where the market has gone since. So below are a few thoughts ahead of Audit and Risk on 15 September. You're not being singled out — every authority gets one of these — and there's no agenda in it.

We wrote because of one number in your Q3 appendix. You publish a PWLB redemption value of £230.512m against £265.969m of principal at 31 December — £35.457m of discount — and a net figure across the whole book of £37.098m after £3.178m of premia. What made us look twice is that the same net figure was £38.416m at 31 March, £43.726m at 30 September and £37.098m at 31 December. A £6.6m swing inside a single quarter.

It has kept moving. Running your PWLB loans through the DMO's premature repayment formula on this afternoon's curve, notice 314/26, we get about £48.585m of discount on a balance of £255.133m. Same scope as your own PWLB-only figure, eight months later and on a smaller balance because loans have amortised and matured in between. Most of it sits in a handful of long ones — roughly £12.9m on the £25m at 2.32% running to March 2068, about £6.8m on the £15m at 2.67% to 2065, another £6.3m on the £10m at 1.67% to 2069.

We're not suggesting anything follows from that. We don't sell treasury products, we model no MRP and no accounting treatment, and whether a discount is worth acting on turns entirely on replacement cost, which we don't model either. The DMO's quote is the only one that binds; ours is indicative and we say so on the page. The only point we'd make is the one your own quarterly series already makes: a number that moves £6.6m between two reports is a number that is more useful seen daily than quarterly. We compute it every morning for every council, and yours is at pwlbtoday.org/loan-analysis.

The other thing we noticed is in the March strategy report, and it's not about rates at all. Table 1 sets out MRP under five different regimes at once — 4% of CFR for Allerdale's and Copeland's pre-2008 supported expenditure, 3% of opening CFR net of Adjustment A for Carlisle, 2% straight line net of Adjustment A for Cumbria County Council with the bolt-on for the 2016-17 policy change, and Option 3 asset life for everything since 1 April 2023. Three years after reorganisation each predecessor's policy is still travelling with its debt. We've now read enough post-reorganisation authorities to say that is a common position rather than an odd one, and it is very badly served by the training that exists, because almost all of it assumes a single policy on a single CFR.

Which is where the academy comes in. Four courses fit Cumberland squarely: PWLB break costs — mechanics & live calculator, which is the engine above with the workings shown; Debt restructuring next to it; MRP — policy options and revenue impact; and Devolution & reorganisation: the treasury view, which is written for exactly the five-regime problem in your Table 1. All 115 courses are free to local authorities until the end of September at pwlbtoday.org/academy, and free accounts for the whole team.

One last piece of market context for the September report. Bank Rate is 3.75%, ten-year certainty closed at 5.83% and twenty-year at 6.38% this afternoon, and July's sector borrowing was £368m across 33 loans from just 19 borrowers at an average 5.02% — a thin month, which matters if any replacement borrowing is in prospect. That breakdown is at pwlbtoday.org/pwlb-activity.

And if you do find it useful, mentioning it to others would help us more than anything. We're small, word of mouth is most of our marketing, and every sign-up helps us prove the need.

Sign up free → https://pwlbtoday.org/
Follow on LinkedIn → https://www.linkedin.com/company/pwlbtoday/

Russell
